INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
Constitutional Accountability Center (CAC) is a
think tank and public interest law firm dedicated to
fulfilling the progressive promise of the Constitution’s
text and history.  CAC works in our courts, through
our government, and with legal scholars to improve
understanding of the Constitution and preserve the
rights and freedoms it guarantees.  CAC has a strong
interest in ensuring that the Elections Clause is interpreted in a manner consistent with its text and history
and accordingly has an interest in this case.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Exercising its authority under the Elections
Clause, Congress passed the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) in 1993 to increase political participation by eligible citizens and simplify voter registration proces ses across the nation.  To further these
goals, the NVRA directed the Elections Assistance
Commission (EAC) to create a federal “mail voter registration application form” that states must “accept
and use” to register voters.  52 U.S.C. § 20505(a)(1); see
also id. § 20508(a), (b) (detailing EAC’s obligation to
“develop a mail voter registration application form for
elections for Federal office” and prescribing its contents).  The NVRA also authorized states to “ develop
and use a mail voter registration form that meets all
of the criteria” applicable to the federal form.  Id.
§ 20505(a)(2); see also id. § 20506(6)(A)(ii) (requiring a

1 Under Rule 37.6 of the Rules of this Court, amicus states that
no counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in part, and
no counsel or party made a monetary contribution intended to
fund the preparation or submission of this brief.  No person other
than amicus or its counsel made a monetary contribution to its
preparation or submission.

2

state voter registration agency to distribute a form
“equivalent” to the federal form).
Under the NVRA, both the federal form and any
state-developed federal voter registration form  (1)
“may require only such identifying information . . . as
is necessary to enable the appropriate State election
official to assess the eligibility of the applicant and to
administer voter registration and other parts of the
election process”; (2) “shall  include a statement
that . . . specifies each eligibility requirement (including citizenship)”; “contains an attestation that the applicant meets each such requirement”; and “ requires
the signature of the applicant, under penalty of perjury”; and (3) “may not include any requirement for notarization or other formal authentication.”  Id.
§ 20508(b)(1), (2), (3);  id. § 20505(a)(2).  Congress insisted on these strictures to “increase the number of
eligible citizens who register to vote in elections for
Federal office,” while also “protect[ing] the integrity of
the electoral process.”  Id. § 20501(b)(1), (3).2
In Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Arizona, Inc.,
570 U.S. 1 (2013), this Court held that the NVRA
preempted Arizona’s documentary proof of citizenship
requirement, holding that “the fairest reading of the
statute is that a state -imposed requirement of evidence of citizenship not required by the Federal Form
is ‘inconsistent with’ the NVRA’s mandate that States

2 The Act also contains limits on removing voters from registration rolls, including by providing that “[a] State shall complete,
not later than 90 days prior to the date of a primary or general
election for Federal office, any program the purpose of which is to
systematically remove the names of ineligible voters from the official lists of eligible voters.”  Id. § 20507(c)(2)(A).  This brief does
not address the parties’ dispute over the meaning of this provision.

3

‘accept and use’ the Federal Form.”  Id. at 15 (quoting
Ex parte Siebold, 100 U.S. 371 , 397 (1879)).  Because
the NVRA requires that any state form used to register
voters for federal elections comply with the requirements applicable to the federal form, see 52 U.S.C.
§ 20505(a)(2) (requiring state form to comply with requirements for the federal form in § 20508(b)), Arizona
may not require  that eligible citizens provide documentary proof of citizenship when registering to vote
in federal elections using the state form.
Petitioner and its amici, however, assert that despite what the NVRA says, states may refuse to register qualified voters who fill out Arizona’s state voter
registration form unless they  submit documentary
proof of citizenship.  According to Petitioner, even
though the statute requires  only “an attestation that
the applicant meets each such requirement” and prohibits demands for “formal authentication,”
id. § 20508(b)(2), (3), the NVRA must be interpreted to
allow Arizona and other states to require documentary
proof of citizenship to avoid raising doubts about its
constitutionality.  In its view, Congress lacks the
power to override the state’s considered view about
how to enforce its voter qualifications in elections for
federal office .  Pet’r Br. 32-33; Miss. et al. Br. 4 -12;
Claremont Br. 5-13; Center for Election Confidence Br.
14-18; Judicial Watch et al. Br. 9-21; ACLJ et al. Br. 4-
10. This argument cannot be squared with the text and
history of the Elections Clause.
More than two centuries ago, the Constitution’s
Framers concluded that Congress must have the final
say over the mechanics of federal elections .  After
lengthy debates over the Elections Clause—beginning
at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia  and
continuing in the state ratifying conventions and
through the debates over the amendments to the

4

Constitution proposed in 1789—the Framers conferred
on Congress the power to “make or alter” state election
law in order to protect the right to vote in federal elections and allow Congress to set uniform rules for the
time, place, and manner of those elections.  U.S. Const.
art. I § 4, cl. 1.  Where Congress invokes its power to
“make or alter” state law, federal law expressly
preempts state time, place, and manner regulation s,
ensuring that states do not interfere with the people’s
right to vote for their federal representatives.   While
voter qualifications  in federal  elections are tied to
those used in state legislative elections, Congress has
the final word over the mechanics of federal elections,
including voter registration.  Nothing in the Constitution leaves regulation of federal elections to “the unfettered discretion of state legislatures ,” Inter Tribal
Council, 570 U.S. at 17, and that is true even with respect to the enforcement of voter qualifications.  To the
contrary, whatever power states enjoy to regulate federal elections is subject to Congress’s paramount, supervisory power.  Congress was, as one court put it,
“given the whip hand.”  Ass’n of Cmty. Orgs. for Reform
Now v. Edgar, 56 F.3d 791, 794 (7th Cir. 1995).
As this Court has recognized, the Elections Clause
“was the Framers’ insurance against the possibility
that a State would refuse to provide for the election of
representatives to the Federal Congress,” Inter Tribal
Council, 570 U.S.  at 8, and it provides a “safeguard
against manipulation of electoral rules by politicians
and factions in the States to entrench themselves or
place their interests over those of the electorate,” Ariz.
State Legislature v. Ariz. Indep. Redistricting Comm’n,
576 U.S. 787, 815  (2015); U.S. Term Limits , Inc . v.
Thornton, 514 U.S. 779, 808 (1995) (Elections Clause
was a necessary “safeguard against state abuse”).  The
Framers wrote the Elections Clause using “words of

5

great latitude,” because “[i]t was impossible to foresee
all the abuses that might be made of the [States’] discretionary power.”  2 The Records of the Federal Convention of 1787, at 240 (Max Farrand ed., 1911) [hereinafter Farrand’s Records].  As this Court has repeatedly held, “[t]he Clause’s substantive scope is broad.
‘Times, Places, and Manner’ . . . are ‘comprehensive
words,’ which ‘embrace authority to provide a complete
code for congressional elections,’ including .  . . regulations relating to ‘registration.’”  Inter Tribal Council,
570 U.S. at 8-9 (quoting Smiley v. Holm, 285 U.S. 355,
366 (1932)).   “As Alexander Hamilton put it, the Constitution lodges power over congressional elections in
state legislatures ‘primarily’ and in Congress ‘ultimately.’”   Watson v. Republican Nat’l Comm. , 146 S.
Ct. 2165, 2170 (2026) (quoting The Federalist No. 59 ,
at 362 (Alexander Hamilton) (Clinton Rossiter ed. ,
1961)).
In passing the NVRA, Congress used this express
authority to curb “the steady decline in citizen participation in Federal elections” and make the “registration
process for Federal elections as accessible as possible
while maintaining the integrity of the electoral processes.”  H.R. Rep. No. 103-9, at 3 (1993).  It did so by
establishing new legal safeguards to make voter registration widely accessible to voters possessing the necessary qualifications.   During deliberations about the
Act, Congress considered whether to include a carveout that would permit states to require documentary
proof of citizenship.  It refused to permit such
measures, concluding that such a loophole was not
“necessary or consistent with the purposes of” the
NVRA and “could be interpreted by States to permit
registration requirements that could effectively eliminate, or seriously interfere with, the mail registration
program of the Act.”  H.R. Rep. No. 103-66, at 23 (1993)

6

(Conf. Rep.).  Instead, Congress adopted language that
only requires “an attestation that the applicant meets
[eligibility] requirement [s],” signed under penalty of
perjury, and prohibits demands for “formal authentication.”  52 U.S.C. § 20508(b)(2), (3).
Exercising its power under the Elections Clause,
Congress determined that more intrusive voter registration rules, such as demands for documentary proof
of citizenship, were an unjustifiable barrier to the
right to vote in federal elections.  Arizona plainly disagrees, but “the Constitution explicitly gives Congress
the final say” on that question.  Foster v. Love, 522 U.S.
67, 72 (1997).  Because Arizona’s documentary proof of
citizenship requirement cannot be squared with the
command of the NVRA, the judgment of the court of
appeals should be affirmed.
ARGUMENT
I. The Text and History of the Elections
Clause Make Clear that the Elections
Clause Gives Congress Broad Power to
Override State Law in Order to Protect the
Right to Vote in Federal Elections.
1. The Elections Clause provides that “[t]he Times,
Places and Manner of holding Elections for Senators
and Representatives, shall be prescribed in each State
by the Legislature thereof; but the Congress may at
any time by Law make or alter such Regulations, except as to the Places of chusing Senators.”  U.S. Const.
art. I, § 4, cl. 1.  The plain text of the Elections Clause
serves “two functions.  Upon the States it imposes the
duty (‘shall be prescribed’) to prescribe the time, place,
and manner of electing Representatives and Senators;
upon Congress it confers the power to alter those regulations or supplant them altogether.”  Inter Tribal

7

Council, 570 U.S. at 8; see 4 The Debates in the Several
State Conventions on the Adoption of the Federal Constitution 62 (Jonathan Elliot ed. , 1836) [hereinafter
“Elliot’s Debates ”] (“[I]n the first part of the clause,
th[e] power over elections is given to the states, and in
the latter part the same power is given to Congress.”);
id. at 68 (explaining that the Elections Clause “enables
Congress to alter such regulations as the states shall
have made with respect to elections ”).  Thus, even
though voting qualifications in federal elections were
explicitly tied in the Constitution to those “requisite
for Electors of the most numerous branch of the State
Legislature,” U.S. Const. art. I, § 2, cl. 1, Congress
would possess a veto over all state regulation of the
mechanics of federal elections.
The Framers gave Congress th is “final say,” Foster, 522 U.S. at 72, over the broad mechanics of federal
elections in order to empower Congress to “intervene
against acts of injustice within the states,” Jack N. Rakove, Original Meanings: Politics and Ideas in the
Making of the Constitution 224 (1996), and to establish
uniform rules that fulfilled the Constitution’s promise
of popular sovereignty by “We the People,” The Federalist No. 57, supra, at 351 (James Madison) (“Who are
to be the electors of the federal representatives?  Not
the rich, more than the poor; not the learned, more
than the ignorant; not the haughty heirs of distinguished names, more than the humble sons of obscure
and unpropitious fortune.  The electors are to be the
great body of the people of the United States.”).
The Framers were concerned that if Congress did
not have the express power to “make or alter” state
election law, states would use their power to regulate
the time, place, and manner of federal elections to
deny or abridge the right of eligible voters to freely select federal representatives of their choice.   “The

8

dominant purpose of the Elections Clause, the historical record bears out, was to empower Congress to override state election rules, ” Ariz. State Legislature , 576
U.S. at 814-15, a reflection of “the Framers’ distrust of
the States regarding elections,” U.S. Term Limits, 514
U.S. at 811 n.21 ; Eliza Sweren -Becker & Michael
Waldman, The Meaning, History, and Importance of
the Elections Clause, 96 Wash. L. Rev. 997, 999 (2021)
(“[S]uspicion of those very legislators suffuses the purpose and history of the Clause.”) ; id. at 1010 (the
Founding generation feared that giving unbounded
power to state legislatures would enable “powerful factions within states . . . to gerrymander districts and
entrench their power”).
As James Madison put it, the grant of power to
Congress to override state regulation of the time,
place, and manner of federal elections was necessary
because “State Legislatures will sometimes fail or refuse to consult the common interest at the expense of
their local conveniency  or prejudices.”  2 Farrand’s
Records, supra, at 240; see Franita Tolson, Reinventing
Sovereignty?: Federalism as a Constraint on the Voting
Rights Act, 65 Vand. L. Rev. 1195, 1226 (2012) (discussing “the delegates’ fear that the states, had they
been in complete control of elections, could have used
this power to the detriment of their citizens, who
would have little recourse ”).  Madison explained that
“the Legislatures of the States ought not to have the
uncontrouled right of regulating the times places &
manner of holding elections.”  2 Farrand’s Records, supra, at 240.  To prevent abuse s by the states, it was
necessary to give “a controuling power to the Natl.
Legislature.”  Id. at 241.
Madison was particularly concerned that states
would use their power to regulate elections to skew the
outcomes of federal elections.  “Whenever the State

9

Legislatures had a favorite measure to carry, they
would take care so to mould their regulations as to favor the candidates they wished to succeed.”  Id.
Along similar lines, Gouverneur Morris observed that
“the States might make false returns and then make
no provisions for new elections.”  Id.; see The Federalist
No. 59, supra, at 363 (Alexander Hamilton) (arguing
that, without the Elections Clause, states “could at any
moment annihilate [the Union] by neglecting to provide for the choice of persons to administer its affairs”).
The Elections Clause was the “Framers’ insurance
against th[is] possibility.”  Inter Tribal Council , 570
U.S. at 8.  By the close of debate , the Convention’s
overwhelming consensus was that the Constitution
should “give the Natl. legislature a power not only to
alter the provisions of the States, but [also] to make
regulations in case the States should fail or refuse altogether.”  2 Farrand’s Records, supra, at 242.  As one
influential delegate to the Pennsylvania Convention
explained, in case “the State governments may abuse
their power, and regulate these elections in such manner as would be highly inconvenient to the people,” the
Elections Clause gave Congress the express “constitutional power of correcting them.”  Letter from Timothy
Pickering, Delegate, Pa. Ratifying Convention, to
Charles Tillinghast (Dec. 24, 1787), quoted in Charles
W. Upham, 2 The Life of Timothy Pickering 357 (1873).
2. At the Founding, the breadth of Congress’s express power to “make or alter” state regulation of federal elections was understood by supporters and detractors alike.  The plain text of the Elections Clause,
as James Madison explained at the Constitutional
Convention, uses “words of great latitude,” recognizing
that “[i]t was impossible to foresee all the abuses that
might be made of the [states’] discretionary power.”  2
Farrand’s Records , supra, at 240.  As Madison

10

explained, “[w]hether the electors should vote by ballot
or vivâ  voce, should assemble at this place or that
place; should be divided into districts or all meet at one
place, shd all vote for all the representatives; or all in
a district vote for a number allotted to the district;
these & many other points would depend on the Legislatures[] and might materially affect the appointments.”  Id. at 240-41.
Thus, the Framers’ understanding was that Congress would have the final say over questions of balloting, location of polling places, districting, and other of
“the numerous requirements as to procedure and safeguards which experience shows are necessary in order
to enforce the fundamental right involved.”  Smiley,
285 U.S. at 366.  That includes voter registration, as
this Court has held.  See Inter Tribal Council, 570 U.S.
at 9; U.S. Br. 5 (“The power to regulate the ‘Manner’ of
an election includes the power to regulate the registration of voters. ”); see also Rob Natelson, The Original
Scope of the Congressional Power to Regulate Elections, 13 U. Pa. J. Const. L. 1, 12 (2010) (noting that in
the Founding-era “English, Scottish, and Irish sources
used the phrase ‘manner of election’” to include “provisions for registration lists” and that “Americans ascribed the same general content to the phrase”).
Opponents of the Elections Clause, too, understood
that the Clause gave Congress sweeping power to regulate the time, place, and manner of federal elections,
explaining that their “great difficulty” was that “the
power given by the 4 th section was unlimited,” 2 Elliot’s Debates, supra, at 25, and “admits of the most
dangerous latitude,” 3 id. at 175; 4 id. at 55 (“[T]hey
are words of very great extent.  This clause provides
that a Congress may at any time alter such regulations, except as to the places of choosing senators.”).

11

3. In the ensuing debates over ratification of the
Constitution, the Elections C lause was vigorously debated, but both sides understood the breadth of power
the Clause gave Congress over elections.
Anti-Federalists argued that the Elections Clause
“strike[s] at the state legislatures, and .  . . take[s]
away that power of [elections] which reason dictates
they ought to have among themselves.”  4 id. at 51.  In
their view, “Congress ought not to have the power to
control elections.”  2 id. at 23.
Pressed to persuade their fellow Americans that
the Elections Clause should be included in the Constitution, the Constitution’s supporters justified “Congress’s power over elections as a way of correcting unjust state voting systems and defending the people’s
right to equal voting power.”  Pauline Maier, Ratification: The People Debate the Constitution, 1787-1788, at
210 (2010).  In other words, they did not disagree that
the Clause gave great power to Congress; they simply
argued that it was appropriate for the Constitution to
do so.
For example, in the Virginia ratifying convention,
James Madison stressed that Congress ought to have
a role in securing equal voting rights .  “Some states
might regulate the elections on the principles of equality, and others might regulate them otherwise.  This
diversity would be obviously unjust. . . .  Should the
people of any state by any means be deprived of the
right of suffrage, it was judged proper that it should be
remedied by the ge neral government.”  3 Elliot’s Debates, supra, at 367.  Others worried that states would
simply not hold elections for federal office, preventing
the popular vote demanded by the Constitution.  Id. at
10 (“If the state legislature . . . would not appoint a
place for holding elections, then there might be no election . . . .”).  These abuses “could only be guarded

12

against by giving this discretionary power, to the Congress, of altering the time, place, and manner of holding the elections.”  Id.
Likewise, in the Massachusetts Convention, Theophilus Parsons argued that the Elections Clause was
necessary to “secur[e] to the people their equal rights
of election ,” 2 id. at 26, observing that the grant of
power to Congress provided a check against partisan
manipulation of the electoral process.  “[W]hen faction
and party spirit run high,” Parsons worried, states
might “introduce such regulations as would render the
rights of the people insecure and of little value.  They
might make an unequal and partial division of the
states into districts for the election of representatives,
or they might even disqualify one third of the electors.”
Id. at 27.  “Without these powers in Congress, the people can have no remedy; but the 4th section provides a
remedy, a controlling power in a legislature  . . . who
will hear impartially, and preserve and restore to the
people their equal and sacred rights of election.”  Id.;
see id. at 25-26 (Mr. Cabot) (arguing that the Elections
Clause was “as highly prized as any [section] in the
Constitution” because “the right of electing persons to
represent the people in the federal government” is “an
important and sacred right”  (quotation marks omitted)); id. at 51 (arguing that, because of inequality of
representation in South Carolina, “representatives . . .
from that state, will not be chosen  by the people , but
will be the representatives of a faction of that state.  If
the general government cannot control in this case,
how are the people secure?”).3

3 Similar arguments in favor of federal power over federal elections were made in other state ratifying conventions as well.  See
2 Elliot’s Debates, supra, at 441 (arguing that, in the event a state
legislature should order a state -wide election to be held in one
city, “ought not the general government to have the power to alter

13

Madison and others also stressed the importance
of establishing uniform ground rules in federal elections.  At the Virginia ratifying convention, Madison
argued that “the regulation of time, place, and manner, of electing the representatives, should be uniform
throughout the continent.”  3 id. at 367.  In other
states, too, the Constitution’s supporters argued that
such regulations “ought to be uniform, and the elections held on the same day throughout the United
States, to prevent corruption or undue influence.”  2
id. at 535; see 4 id. at 60 (“Uniformity in matters of
election is also of the greatest consequence.  They
ought all to be judged by the same law and the same
principles, and not to be different in one state from
what they are in another. . . .  It will be more convenient to have the manner uniform in all the states.”);
Letter from Timothy Pickering to Charles Tillinghast
(Dec. 24, 1787), supra, at 357 (“[I]f any particular State
government should be refractory, and . . . either make
no such regulations or improper ones, then the Congress will have power to make such regulations as will
ensure to the people their rights of election and establish a uniformity in the mode of constituting the members of the Senate and House of Representatives.”).
Thus, throughout the ratifying debates, supporters of the Constitution made the case that a congressional veto over state regulation of the time, place, and

such improper election of one of its own constituent parts?”); 4 id.
at 53 -54 (recognizing the need for an “ultimate power in Congress” in case “a few powerful states should combine , and make
regulations concerning elections which might deprive many of the
electors of a fair exercise of their rights”); id. at 303 (“it is absolutely necessary that Congress should have this superintending
power, lest, by the intrigues of a ruling faction in a state , the
members of the House of Representatives should not really represent the people of the state”).

14

manner of holding elections was necessary because
state legislatures could not be trusted to “secur[e] to
the people their equal rights of election.”  2 Elliot’s Debates, supra, at 26.  These arguments carried the day,
establishing the constitutional framework for federal
regulation of federal elections that still governs  more
than two centuries later.
4. The First Congress  reaffirmed the need for
broad federal veto power over state regulation of the
time, place, and manner of federal elections.  The
members of the First Congress, many of whom had
played a critical role in the framing of the Constitution, rejected a proposed amendment to the Elections
Clause, which would have permitted Congress to regulate the time, place, and manner of federal elections
only when a “State shall refuse or neglect, or be unable
. . . to make such election.”  1 Annals of Cong.  797
(1789) (Joseph Gales ed., 1834).
In the debates over the proposal to eliminate Congress’s power to “alter” state regulation , Madison argued that “the constitution stands very well as it is”
and that the proposed amendment would “tend to destroy the principles and  the efficacy of the constitution.”  Id. at 798, 800.  The Elections Clause was “one
of the most justifiable of all the powers of Congress; it
was essential to a body representing the whole community, that they should have power to regulate their
own elections, in order to secure a representation from
every part, and prevent any improper regulations.”  Id.
at 797.
5. And in the years since, this Court has repeatedly
confirmed what the Constitution’s text and history
make clear: the Constitution provides for broad congressional power to regulate the time, place, and manner of federal elections in order to “override state election rules,” and “a ct as a safeguard against

15

manipulation of electoral rules by politicians and factions in the States to entrench themselves or place
their interests over those of the electorate.”  Ariz. State
Legislature, 576 U.S. at 814 -15; Inter Tribal Council ,
570 U.S. at 8-9; U.S. Term Limits, 514 U.S. at 808-09;
see also Rucho v. Common Cause, 588 U.S. 684, 697-98
(2019).
And for more than a century, this Court has recognized the Clause’s preemptive force, holding that
“when Congress legislates with respect to the ‘Times,
Places and Manner’ of holding congressional elections,
it necessarily displaces some element of a pre-existing
legal regime erected by the States.”  Inter Tribal Council, 570 U.S. at 14; see also Siebold, 100 U.S. at 384
(“[T]he power of Congress over the subject [of federal
elections] is paramount. . . .   When exercised, the action of Congress, so far as it extends and conflicts with
the regulations of the State, necessarily supersedes
them.  This is implied in the power to ‘make or alter.’”);
Smiley, 285 U.S. at 366-67 (“Congress may supplement . . . state regulations or may substitute its own.
It may impose additional penalties . . . or provide independent sanctions.  It ‘has a general supervisory power
over the whole subject.’” (quoting Siebold, 100 U.S. at
387)).
In sum, “the power the Elections Clause confers is
none other than the power to pre -empt.”  Inter Tribal
Council, 570 U.S. at 14; see also Franita Tolson, Election Law “Federalism” and the Limits of the Antidiscrimination Framework, 59 Wm. & Mary L. Rev. 2211,
2217 (2018) (“The breadth of congressional power under the Clause lies in Congress ’s ability to veto state
law at will, a feature that is at odds with most of the
prevailing views of federalism.”).

16

II. The National Voter Registration Act’s Guarantees Designed to Increase Voter Registration in Federal Elections Fall Squarely
Within Congress’s Express Power to Alter
State Regulation of the Time, Place, and
Manner of Federal Elections.
In enacting the NVRA, Congress used its express
constitutional authority to “alter” state voter registration rules applicable to federal elections, preempting
laws, like Arizona’s, that make it more difficult for eligible citizens to register to vote in federal elections.
Indeed, during the debates over its passage, the
NVRA’s supporters considered and rejected the argument that states should be able to demand that eligible
voters provide documentary proof of citizenship in order to register to vote in federal elections.  Refusing to
permit states to impose burdensome obstacles to registering to vote in federal elections, Congress required
that registration forms “include a statement that  . . .
specifies each eligibility requirement (including citizenship),” “contains an attestation that the applicant
meets each such requirement,” and “ requires the signature of the applicant, under penalty of perjury ,” 52
U.S.C. § 20508(b)(2), while also prohibiting “any requirement for notarization or other formal authentication,” id. § 20508(b)(3).  As this statutory text reflects,
Congress concluded that state documentary proof of
citizenship requirements went beyond what is “necessary to enable the appropriate State election official to
assess the eligibility of the applicant,” id.
§ 20508(b)(1).
Members of Congress repeatedly emphasized the
importance of the NVRA ’s reforms to protecting the
right to vote of all eligible citizens.  See, e.g., 139 Cong.
Rec. 2427 (1993) (Rep. Rush) (“The right to vote is a
fundamental right in America.  It is the duty of the

17

Federal Government to protect this right.  The [NVRA]
provides simple and effective means to ensure this
right for all Americans.”); id. at 2431 (Rep. Hilliard)
(the NVRA “will extend democracy to everyone”); id. at
5223 (Sen. Kennedy) (“The right to vote is the cornerstone of our democracy.  Without it, all our other rights
are in danger.”).  They also underscored that “[d]eclining voter participation jeopardizes the very roots of our
democratic system.”  Id. at 5227 (Sen. Rockefeller).  As
Senator Rockefeller explained, “ [c]onfusing registration forms, lack of convenient access to registration offices, and demanding registration requirements have
led to the ineffectiveness of our current registration
system.”  Id.  Another congressman put it succinctly:
“If we care about a healthy, participatory democracy in
its fullest sense, it’s imperative that we facilitate voter
registration.”  Id. at 2435 (Rep. Becerra); see also id. at
9222 (Rep. Kleczka) (“Congress has the responsibility
to make the registration process as easy as possible.”).
Not all members of Congress, however, supported
the NVRA’s measures to increase voter registration.
Some voiced concerns that easing voter registration
procedures would open the door to noncitizens voting
in federal elections.  See, e.g., id. at 2450 (Rep. Canaday) ( asserting that “millions of illegal aliens and
other noncitizens will flood into the American electoral
system”); id. at 2443 (Rep. Bachus)  (arguing that the
NVRA “will result in the registration of .  . . illegal aliens”).  The Act’s champions, however, believed that
the bill’s measures protecting against noncitizen registration were sufficient and that worries about noncitizen voting were exaggerated.  See id. at 5224 (Sen.
Kennedy) (“The contention that the bill will encourage
voter fraud or voting by noncitizens is simply wrong.
The bill requires everyone who applies to register to
vote to attest that they are U.S. citizens and are

18

eligible to vote.”); id. at 9224 (Rep. Swift) (“The fact is
that this legislation contains for the first time in the
history of the U.S. [f]ederal law that will provide criminal penalties for fraudulently registering to vote.”).
Questions about permissible citizenship verification measures came to a head in the Senate.  After the
NVRA passed the House, the Senate passed a version
of the bill that included a “rule of construction” providing that “[n]othing in this Act shall be cons trued to
preclude a State from requiring presentation of documentary evidence of the citizenship of an applicant for
voter registration.”  Id. at 5098; see id. at 5099 (amendment agreed to).  Some Senators expressed concerns
about this provision and pressed the Conference Committee to address it.  See id. at 5232 (Sen. Simon)
(“This bill safeguards against the potential problem
and the provision permitting States to require documentary evidence of citizenship at registration time is
at best unnecessary and at worst may be implemented
in a discriminatory fashion that may violate the Voting
Rights Act.  Accordingly, it is my hope the conferees
look at this provision closely and seriously reconsider
it.”).
The House and Senate versions of the bills were
subsequently conferenced, and the Conference Committee deleted this amendment.  As the Committee explained, the amendment was “not necessary or consistent with the purposes of” the NVRA and “could be
interpreted by States to permit registration requirements that could effectively eliminate, or seriously interfere with, the mail registration program of the Act.”
H.R. Rep. No. 103 -66, at 23  (Conf. Rep).  In its final
form, the NVRA demanded states use registration
forms that required voters to attest to their eligibility
under penalty of perjury , but  did not permit more

19

burdensome demands for proof such as those contained in the Arizona law at issue here.
Petitioner and its amici, however, contend that the
decision below, which read s the NVRA in a manner
consistent with its text and history, “runs headlong
into Arizona’s power over voter qualifications.”  Pet’r
Br. 32.  This is wrong.
First, the NVRA does not in any manner regulate
voter qualifications established by the states.  It “regulate[s] how federal elections are held, . . . not who may
vote in them.”  Inter Tribal Council , 570 U.S. at 16.
The NVRA leaves the setting of voter qualifications to
the states and operates on the assumption that citizenship—the qualification at issue here —is a necessary
qualification for suffrage.  See 52 U.S.C. § 20508(b)(2).
And its statutory scheme leaves states with ample
tools to enforce their chosen voter qualifications.  See
Inter Tribal Council , 570 U.S. at 15.  To be sure, the
NVRA may have an impact on how states enforce their
voter qualifications, but that is a natural consequence
of the fact that the Constitution gives Congress —not
the states, and not this Court —the final say over the
mechanics of federal elections , including voter registration.  See Watson, 146 S. Ct. at 2181.
Second, the Constitution does not contain any freestanding grant of power to the states to enforce voter
qualifications in elections for federal office.  Of course,
the Constitution ’s Voter Qualification Clause  “t[ies]
the federal franchise to the state franchise,” Inter
Tribal Council, 570 U.S. at 17 , but it does not grant
any additional powers to states to regulate federal
elections.  Whatever power states enjoy to  enforce
their chosen voter qualifications —whether through
voter registration rules or otherwise —comes from the
Elections Clause and is subject to Congress’s  paramount, supervisory “make or alter” power.  Nothing in

20

the Constitution leaves regulation of federal elections
to “the unfettered discretion of state legislatures.”  Id.
Petitioner’s constitutional attack on the NVRA
thus turns a blind eye to the text and history of the
Elections Clause.  As discussed above, t he “substantive scope” of that text is “broad” and plainly includes
“regulations relating to ‘registration.’”  Id. at 8-9 (quoting Smiley, 285 U.S. at 366) .  And its history reflects
the Framers’ judgment that “it was essential to a body
representing the whole community, that they should
have the power to regulate their own elections, in order to secure a representation from every part, and
prevent any improper regulations.”  1 Annals of Cong.,
supra, at 797.  That is why the Framers rejected proposed amendments that would have stripped from the
Elections Clause the power to “alter” state time, place,
and manner regulation of federal elections.  Petitioner
and its amici simply cannot come to grips with the veto
power the Constitution confers on Congress.
For good reason, this Court has long held that the
“power of Congress . . . ‘is paramount, and may be exercised at any time, and to any extent which it deems
expedient; and so far as it is exercised, and no farther,
the regulations effected supersede those of the State
which are inconsistent therewith.’”  Inter Tribal Council, 570 U.S. at 9  (quoting Siebold, 100 U.S. at 392).
Far from being limited in purpose or narrow in scope,
the Elections Clause gives Congress a sweeping power
to “secur[e] to the people their equal rights of election,”
2 Elliot’s Debates, supra, at 26, in choosing federal representatives.  Congress sought to protect this right in
the NVRA, requiring states to utilize simple, easily understandable voter registration forms to increase the
number of eligible citizens registered to vote and
preempting state measures , like the Arizona law at

21

issue here, that imposed additional burdens on the
electorate.
In sum, the arguments offered by Petitioner and
its amici to make an end-run around the NVRA’s guarantees are manifestly inconsistent with both the text
and history of the statute and the Elections Clause.
The Elections Clause gives Congress the last word on
the mechanics of federal elections and thus “requires
that Arizona’s rule give way.”  Inter Tribal Council ,
570 U.S. at 15.
CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, the judgment of the
court of appeals should be affirmed.
